SK2133 The called partial method has no implementation

A partial void with no implementing declaration is erased together with every call to it, arguments included, so a call that reads as a hook does nothing at all.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno

Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0
SupersedesS3251

Why

⚠ A `partial` method with no implementation is legal, and erasing it is the feature — so the declaration on its own is never the finding. The call is. When no implementing declaration exists the compiler removes the defining declaration and every call to it, and argument evaluation goes with the call, so work written into an argument silently does not happen. ⚠ Requiring a call is also what makes the rule decidable rather than merely narrow: a classic partial void may carry no accessibility modifier and is therefore implicitly private, so every caller it can ever have is inside the declaring type, which is in this compilation in full. "Nothing calls it" and "something calls it" are both facts here, not guesses about the rest of the world — which is the difference between this rule and the field half of #24, and it is why an unimplemented hook nobody has taken up is left alone.

Example

Instead of:

partial class Importer {
    partial void OnRowRead(Row row);

    void Read() {
        OnRowRead(Parse(next));   // Parse(next) never runs
    }
}

Write:

partial class Importer {
    partial void OnRowRead(Row row);

    void Read() {
        var row = Parse(next);
        OnRowRead(row);
    }
}

partial class Importer {
    partial void OnRowRead(Row row) => log.Add(row);
}

When it does not fire

⚠ The other half of issue #186 is a compile error, and it was verified as one rather than assumed. A C# 9 extended partial method — one with an accessibility modifier, a non-void return type, or an out parameter — must have an implementation, and a probe compiling one without gives CS8795. That half needs no rule and cannot reach a compiling analysis; it is excluded here by requiring void rather than by hoping. On the classic form the same probe draws nothing at all — no CS, no CA, at AnalysisMode=All — which is what makes this the half worth a rule. ⚠ An unimplemented `partial void` that nothing calls is deliberately left alone: it is an extension point nobody has taken up, it costs nothing at runtime, and reporting it would put a finding on the language feature rather than on a mistake. Every part of the declaring type is walked, generated parts included, so a call from generated source counts as a call and an implementation in generated source counts as an implementation — the finding is about a hook the compilation leaves empty, not about one file. Nested types are covered because the walk is over the whole declaration. The side-effect clause in the message is syntactic and deliberately generous — a call, a construction, an await, an assignment or an increment anywhere in an argument is enough — and it changes only the wording, never whether the finding exists, so being wrong in the loud direction costs a sentence rather than a false positive. Report-only, because the two repairs run in opposite directions: writing the implementing part is right when the hook was meant to do something, deleting the declaration and its calls is right when it was not, and nothing in the source says which. Generated code is excluded from reporting.
